sections.name: Hammer
sections.card:
Summary: A close-range item from the Donkey Kong arcade game. Whoever grabs it runs along, swinging it from side to side without pause. It hits extremely hard, but the holder has no recovery move available.
Uses: Grabbing it sends a player into a state that inflicts significant damage and knockback, but while swinging they cannot jump a second time in the air, use any other attacks or defend.
Tips: Sometimes the mallet head falls off as the item is picked up, leaving a useless handle that is still swung for the usual time. From Melee onward the chance is 12.5%, one in eight. The head left on the ground can be grabbed and tossed as a strong item. Against a rival swinging a Hammer, knocking them off a ledge can finish them, because they can neither use special moves nor jump in midair unless they manage to drop it.

sections.name: Beam Sword
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range battering item, similar in appearance to a lightsaber. It can be wielded and charged for melee attacks or thrown, like all other battering items.
Uses: Used as a battering item, it adds to your power and gives you extra choices because it can also be thrown. The blade grows longer the stronger the attack is, so it is longest on a smash attack. Its length also differs from one fighter to the next.
Looks like: A glowing blade that begins about as long as a short sword.
Tips: In Melee its range significantly increases in size, particularly on charged smash attacks. Peach can pull a Beam Sword out with her Vegetable attack, but the chance is slim: 1/768 in Melee.

sections.name: Star Rod
sections.card:
Summary: A magic wand with room for 16 star shots; thrown at someone, it knocks them away at a low angle. It is an odd mix of a battering item and a projectile item.
Uses: Swing it to hit opponents at close range. A smash attack or a tilt instead fires stars that hit from far away. Its strongest use is a smash attack by Captain Falcon or Sheik.
Tips: The item has only sixteen stars, and Captain Falcon's smash attack shoots off 5 stars and Sheik's 2, so they use it up quickly. When it runs out, throwing it at enemies is the more practical option: a thrown Star Rod deals powerful semi-spike knockback that can gimp recoveries or act as a general KO move. The stars are projectiles, so they can be reflected or absorbed.

sections.name: Super Scope
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range shooting item based on a Super Nintendo peripheral. In Melee, tapping the attack button fires three small shots, and holding it charges a stronger, larger shot.
Uses: Tap the attack button repeatedly for a constant stream of small shots that each do little knockback and damage; the high rate of fire gives a trapping effect, as the opponent has little or no time to act. Hold the button to charge a bigger shot. It has limited ammunition, 48 shots in Melee, and different charge levels change the ammo used.
Tips: In Melee the shooter has to stand still while firing. Uncharged shots go through opponents, so one burst can pin down several of them, but their 280 degree knockback angle gives only a feeble meteor smash that does little against anyone near the stage. Once the ammunition is gone it only puffs out smoke, though throwing it still adds a little knockback and damage.

sections.name: Ray Gun
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range weapon that is not very strong, but it fires quickly enough to juggle foes without trouble.
Uses: It holds 16 shots. In Melee each shot deals 4% with horizontal knockback and can be fired every 30 frames, which lets it juggle opponents at low percents or carry them to the blast line at mid percents.
Looks like: Looks like a toy; its green beams are short, thick and highly reflective.
Tips: Moves that reflect or absorb projectiles work on the shots, but a thrown gun can only be reflected.

sections.name: Maxim Tomato and Heart Container
sections.card:
Summary: Two healing items: each reduces the damage percentage of whoever picks it up. In Melee the Maxim Tomato heals 50% of a character's damage percentage and the Heart Container heals a total of 100%.
Uses: A Maxim Tomato does not heal at once: a moment after you eat it, the damage number starts to count down, and picking up another item in the meantime does not stop that. Damage taken while it heals comes off the amount restored, so a 10% hit leaves you with only 40% healed. A Heart Container floats down slowly and takes a full 100 percentage points off your damage.
Looks like: The Maxim Tomato is a small red tomato with a noticeable black and white M on the front.
Tips: In the All-Star Rest Area you are given three Heart Containers that can heal all of your damage instead of the standard 100%. Due to a glitch, entering the teleporter in Melee interrupts a Heart Container's healing, so it does not fully heal you.

sections.name: Metal Box
sections.card:
Summary: A transforming item that debuted in Melee: whoever breaks it becomes a Metal fighter for a short time, much heavier but slower and quicker to fall.
Uses: In Melee the effects last 12 seconds, though the time limit decreases as the fighter takes damage, especially from fire attacks. Walking speed is multiplied by 0.7 and jump force by 1.55, though not by enough to make up for the faster fall.
Tips: The faster fall makes recoveries harder. In Melee, a Metal Box hit by a projectile disappears, but disjointed attacks and any attack from a sword-wielding character still break it and still turn the attacker into a Metal fighter.

sections.name: Super Star (Starman)
sections.card:
Summary: A Mario item, called the Starman in Melee, that shields you from every attack for a short time.
Uses: Whoever grabs it gets ten seconds of invincibility. Melee keeps the first game's behaviour here: touching opponents does not damage them.
Looks like: The fighter who grabs it is given a bright, sparkling appearance.
Tips: It ricochets in big arcs over the field, off platforms and walls, and if nobody gets it soon it drops off the edge of the stage. In Melee, the star's own tune pushes the stage music down until you can barely hear it.

sections.name: Super Mushroom and Poison Mushroom
sections.card:
Summary: Two Mario items that change your size for about ten seconds. The Super Mushroom, which debuted in Melee, makes you giant, and the Poison Mushroom makes you shrink.
Uses: A Super Mushroom makes you bigger, stronger and heavier, so foes have a harder time launching you. In Melee it multiplies your weight by 1.6 and the damage of your direct attacks by 1.2, but it gives no armor, so any knockback still makes you flinch. A Poison Mushroom does the reverse: it makes you smaller and takes weight and attack damage away.
Looks like: The Poison Mushroom is a deceptive look-alike of the Super Mushroom, with a duller color scheme and angry eyes.
Tips: Both keep sliding to the right, but in Melee they slide left if they spawn on the right half of the stage. Touching one while under the effect of the other restores your normal size. In Melee, jumping at the moment a Super Mushroom's effects wear off gives a super jump almost as high as two jumps while wearing the Bunny Hood.

sections.name: Fighting Wire Frames
sections.card:
Summary: Common enemies in Melee's 1-player modes, in male and female varieties. Generally they are weak and light fighters and are very easy to KO.
Weak points: They have no special moves, cannot charge a smash attack, and their attacks are much weaker copies of Captain Falcon's and Zelda's. With no recovery moves, they rely on jumping high. Their hits carry little real force, and they are slow, so they are easy to dodge around.
Looks like: A framework of pink lines in a humanoid shape, with the Super Smash Bros. logo on the face and a red heart-like object in the chest; they are larger than the characters they are modelled on.
Tips: Males always home towards your character, while females play a more passive role and rarely attack directly. In Cruel Melee all of them are extremely aggressive, extremely powerful and harder to knock off-stage, so characters cannot survive easily among them. In Adventure Mode they are fought in a low-gravity version of Battlefield, and there and in Multi-Man Melee they cannot be Star or Screen KO'd.

sections.name: Classic Mode's final boss
sections.card:
Summary: The last fight of Classic Mode, fought on the Melee version of Final Destination. It has a set amount of HP that must be depleted to win, and in Melee that amount depends on the difficulty.
Weak points: In Melee this boss loses the ability to turn around, and its movement depends entirely on the attack it is using and your position: it always returns to its starting position when it is not attacking.
Looks like: A white glove; in Melee its wrist fades into nothingness instead of ending in a cuff.
Tips: Its power increases with each increment in difficulty, and the highest levels give it many attacks that can KO in one hit. It shoots a laser beam from each fingertip, and its gun-shaped hand fires one pair of bullets until it has taken 150% damage and three pairs after that. A slap at the ground buries the player, and its throw into the ground has high damage and knockback but cannot KO under normal conditions. On Normal difficulty or higher, taking half of its HP off within a total of 5 minutes and 50 seconds since the start of Classic Mode brings a second boss into the fight.

sections.name: A hidden boss in Classic Mode
sections.card:
Summary: A bonus boss that can join Classic Mode's last fight alongside the final boss, but only when the conditions the game sets for it are met.
Weak points: It starts with the same number of HP that the first boss started with. Its move where it lies on the ground and has violent spasms cannot hit aerial targets, and the bombs it drops do only low damage with minimal knockback if they hit a character before reaching the ground.
Looks like: Its basic appearance is exactly the same as the final boss's, apart from being a left hand.
Tips: Most of its attacks are stronger variations of the final boss's, plus a few of its own. The fist it flies in with from behind the stage can star KO as low as 35%, its forward throw can KO at low percentages without DI, and the third of its three pokes can star KO at middle to high percentages.

sections.name: Brinstar's rising acid
sections.card:
Summary: Occasionally an earthquake hits Brinstar and acid starts to rise, sometimes covering parts of the stage. The acid deals damage and moderate knockback and will not KO until very high percents, though in Melee a ceiling glitch can make it KO at extremely low percents.
Weak points: While it is rising it generally prevents characters from being KO'd on the bottom blast line. It rises and pauses at various intervals, rarely reaching its highest point, where it covers everything except the topmost platform, and after a while it subsides.
Looks like: Yellow acid, with a large pool of it in the background under a brain-like creature.
Tips: A character who has grabbed the Super Star can avoid the acid. The fleshy parts that hold the stage together can be weakened by attacks, and while they regenerate they are fall-through. In Melee, contact with the acid makes a unique splash effect with a sizzling sound.

sections.name: F-Zero racers on Mute City
sections.card:
Summary: The thirty F-Zero Racers are a hazard on Mute City: they drive around the track continuously, though they only appear on certain segments of the track and at alternating times and laps, and they damage any player on contact, sending them upwards.
Weak points: The racers can be damaged and even destroyed by explosives such as the Motion-Sensor Bomb, powerful attacks and items like the Hammer and Home-Run Bat, and immovable Pokémon like Venusaur or Charizard.
Tips: A destroyed racer's wreckage stays at the point where it exploded for the rest of the match. Touching the track while the platform is hovering over it also damages you. In Adventure Mode's F-Zero stage a giant "!" on the screen warns that cars are approaching, a hit does 35% damage, and you can jump on the pink platforms along the track to avoid them.

sections.name: Pokémon Stadium's changing terrain
sections.card:
Summary: After a varying period of time the stage transforms into a random one of four variants, each based on a Pokémon type, then reverts to the basic form and repeats the cycle. The same variant can occur twice in a row.
Weak points: The fire in the background of the Fire variant is purely aesthetic and has no gameplay effect. On the Water variant's windmill, players on the current lowest arm fall, and in Melee the arms are soft.
Looks like: The basic stage is symmetrical, with one large main platform and two floating soft platforms above it, and a large jumbotron, a crowd and fireworks in the background.
Tips: The jumbotron shows a symbol for the upcoming variation during a stage transition. In Melee tournament play, many players wait out the Fire and Rock transformations by moving to the opposite side of the stage from their opponent until the stage returns to neutral, and many complain that this wastes time. In Melee, on the Fire variant, a character hit towards the right side of the tree's base has a chance of falling through.
